heuristics.rule: Ask target programs for the exact percentage of graduates who obtained tenure-track faculty positions in the last 5 years before assuming academic placement is viable
heuristics.condition: When a prospective PhD student says their goal is to become a professor...
heuristics.action: ...demand the program's actual 5-year tenure-track placement rate; if it exceeds 30%, the program is above average — meaning most programs will be below 30%
heuristics.because: Nationally only 34% of S&E PhDs go to academia at all, and tenure-track is a subset of that; programs rarely volunteer this data, and advisors may have outdated mental models from their own hiring era

heuristics.rule: Add 3-5 years to any biology PhD career timeline to account for mandatory postdoc before competitive faculty candidacy
heuristics.condition: When evaluating time-to-career-stability for biological or biomedical sciences PhDs...
heuristics.action: ...treat the effective career start as 10-12 years post-bachelor's, not 5-6 years, and factor in postdoc-level salaries (~$52,000-$65,000/year) during that period
heuristics.because: 57.8% of bio/biomedical PhDs go directly to postdocs; the postdoc is not optional but a mandatory intermediate step, making the real cost of this path significantly higher than the PhD duration alone suggests

heuristics.rule: Use 'definite commitment at graduation' rate — not eventual employment rate — as the honest metric for program-field career outcomes
heuristics.condition: When comparing career outcomes across fields or programs...
heuristics.action: ...ask what percentage of graduates had committed plans on graduation day, not whether they eventually found employment
heuristics.because: Fields like humanities (65.8%) and biomedical (68.2%) show that over 1 in 3 graduates have no definite plans at graduation, which is the most accurate signal of genuine career risk at the moment it matters most

heuristics.rule: Disregard an advisor's anecdotal academic job market experience if they entered academia before 2010
heuristics.condition: When an advisor or faculty mentor describes academic hiring norms, timelines, or odds...
heuristics.action: ...cross-reference with current NSF SED or equivalent data, not the advisor's personal experience
heuristics.because: Academic placements have dropped 20 percentage points across S&E over 20 years (54% in 2003 to 34% in 2023); advisors who entered in 2005 are working from a mental model that no longer reflects current market conditions

heuristics.rule: Choose CS/Engineering PhD over life sciences PhD when career optionality is a priority
heuristics.condition: When a student is choosing between fields and values having multiple viable career exit points...
heuristics.action: ...weight CS/Engineering more heavily because industry transition requires no retraining or identity shift, whereas biology-to-industry often requires reframing and humanities-to-nonacademic is a cultural identity shift
heuristics.because: Industry/business now employs 47% of new PhDs, but the friction of transition varies dramatically by field; CS PhDs move to industry without postdoc while biology PhDs face retraining barriers and humanities PhDs face institutional culture that actively discourages non-academic paths

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Whether your field mandates a postdoc before permanent employment fundamentally changes the financial and timeline cost of the PhD; it is not a personal choice but a structural requirement in some fields
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check NSF SED postdoc rates for your specific field; rates above 50% (bio: 57.8%, geosciences: 64.2%) signal that postdoc is effectively mandatory, not optional

decision_factors.factor: Definite commitment rate at graduation by field
decision_factors.why_it_matters: This is the most honest available metric of career risk at the point of graduation; a low rate means a meaningful fraction of graduates face genuine uncertainty, not just delayed outcomes
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Reference NSF SED data by field; humanities/arts (65.8%) and biological sciences (68.2%) are lowest, meaning roughly 1 in 3 graduates have no plan on graduation day

decision_factors.factor: 20-year trend direction in academic placements for your target field
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A field where academic placements have fallen 43 percentage points (math/stats) in 20 years has a structurally different risk profile than a field with stable industry demand; the trend tells you whether conditions are getting better or worse
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare the field's 2003 vs. 2023 academic placement rates from NSF SED; math/stats dropped from 70% to 27%, physical sciences from ~55% to ~35%, all S&E from 54% to 34%

decision_factors.factor: Career optionality by field (friction of industry transition)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Not all PhDs transition to industry with equal ease; the cultural, skills-retraining, and identity cost of leaving academia varies enormously by field and affects the real value of the degree
decision_factors.how_to_assess: CS/Engineering: near-zero friction to industry. Biology: moderate retraining required. Humanities: high cultural/identity friction, programs rarely support non-academic paths

decision_factors.factor: Program's actual tenure-track placement rate over the last 5 years
decision_factors.why_it_matters: National averages mask wide program-level variation; a program above 30% tenure-track placement is performing above the national norm and signals a genuinely strong academic pipeline
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the program directly for the count of graduates in the last 5 years who obtained tenure-track positions; divide by total graduates to get the rate; be skeptical of vague or non-specific answers

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The PhD completion date is not the career start date in many fields; the real metric is when you reach financial and professional independence, which is dramatically longer in some fields
decision_factors.how_to_assess: For biology: add 3-5 years postdoc to PhD duration = 10-12 years from bachelor's. For CS: PhD duration is approximately equal to time-to-career. For humanities: add 3-10 years of adjunct/visiting roles

decision_factors.factor: Primary employment destination in your field (academia vs. industry split)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If you plan for academia but 47% of PhDs nationally go to industry — and that share is growing — your planning assumptions may be misaligned with structural market reality
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check NSF SED sector breakdown for your specific field; note that industry now exceeds academia as the primary destination (47% vs. 34%) for S&E PhDs nationally

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing a biology or biomedical sciences PhD with the goal of a faculty position
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You are committing to approximately 10-12 years from bachelor's to independent career, with 3-5 years at postdoc-level salary ($52,000-$65,000/year) in between, and still facing a highly competitive tenure-track market at the end of it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who need visa stability and income certainty; first-generation students without financial cushions to weather a decade of training-level compensation; anyone with dependents or significant financial obligations

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming your advisor's academic career path is a realistic template for your own
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may be planning against a mental model that is 20 years out of date; advisors who entered academia in 2005 experienced a market where 54% of S&E PhDs went to academia — a market that no longer exists
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in any field where academic placements have declined sharply, especially math/stats (70% → 27%) and all S&E fields broadly; students who rely on advisor mentorship rather than independent data gathering

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Over 1 in 3 graduates have no definite plans at graduation (65.8% definite commitment rate); the path to a permanent position commonly involves 3-10 years as adjunct or visiting faculty, and the program culture actively discourages non-academic alternatives rather than supporting them
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone who needs career certainty within a defined timeframe; international students on time-limited visas; students who will accrue opportunity cost relative to entering the workforce directly

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing industry over academia as a PhD career path in biology
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The transition often requires active retraining or reframing of skills, not a seamless pivot — the PhD curriculum and lab culture are optimized for academic outputs, not industry roles
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Biology PhDs who reach the end of a postdoc and decide against faculty positions; students who planned for academia but face a failed job search and must pivot mid-career

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Selecting a PhD program based on advisor reputation without assessing placement outcomes
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A prestigious advisor in a field with structurally declining academic placements does not override the base rate; most labs produce 10+ PhDs per tenure-track slot in biology, regardless of advisor fame
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in competitive life sciences programs where advisor prestige is the primary selection signal; students who conflate advisor success with their own likely outcome

failure_patterns.pattern: Planning an academic career using the advisor's hiring-era mental model rather than current market data
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Advisors are the most accessible source of career guidance and have strong incentives to believe their path is replicable; students defer to authority rather than seeking independent data
failure_patterns.consequence: Students build 5-10 year PhD plans optimized for an academic job market that has contracted by 20+ percentage points since their advisor graduated, resulting in misaligned preparation and genuine career shock at graduation
warning_signs: Advisor entered academia before 2010 and describes the academic job market as 'difficult but manageable'
Program materials emphasize faculty placement without citing actual placement rates or recent years' data

failure_patterns.pattern: Underestimating total time-to-career in biology by treating PhD completion as the career start date
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Program marketing, personal planning, and social framing all treat the PhD as the endpoint; the mandatory postdoc is structurally embedded but rarely foregrounded in recruitment conversations
failure_patterns.consequence: Students accept biology PhDs without financially or psychologically accounting for 3-5 additional years at ~$52,000-$65,000/year before reaching competitive candidacy for permanent positions
warning_signs: Student describes their career plan as 'finish PhD then get a faculty job' without mentioning postdoc
Financial planning only covers PhD stipend years, not post-PhD training period

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating 'eventually got a job' as equivalent to 'had strong outcomes at graduation'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Programs report outcomes in ways that obscure timing; 'all our graduates are employed' is technically true but may describe outcomes 2-5 years after graduation, not at the moment of graduation
failure_patterns.consequence: Students enter high-uncertainty fields (humanities: 65.8% definite commitment, biomedical: 68.2%) without understanding that more than 1 in 3 of their peers will face genuine plan-lessness on graduation day
warning_signs: Program outcome reports describe employment rates without specifying the timeframe after graduation
Student cannot find data on what percentage of graduates had committed plans at the time of degree conferral

failure_patterns.pattern: Selecting a biology or humanities PhD without modeling the non-academic career transition cost
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students self-select into fields based on intellectual interest and assume career pivots are straightforward; program culture reinforces the idea that the academic path is the primary or most natural one
failure_patterns.consequence: Biology PhDs who pivot to industry face active retraining; humanities PhDs face a cultural and identity shift that their programs rarely support, adding friction and delay to already uncertain timelines
warning_signs: Student's entire career contingency plan is 'if academia doesn't work out, I'll go to industry' without any specifics
Program has no structured career development resources for non-academic paths

failure_patterns.pattern: Using national average academic placement rates as reassurance without checking field-specific or program-specific rates
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Aggregate statistics feel more stable and less alarming; students anchor on 'PhDs do well' without disaggregating by field, where math/stats went from 70% to 27% academic placement in 20 years
failure_patterns.consequence: Students in fields with catastrophic academic placement declines make decisions based on cross-field averages that mask the severity of their specific field's restructuring
warning_signs: Student cites broad 'PhDs have low unemployment rates' statistics when asked about academic job prospects
Student in math, statistics, or physical sciences is unaware of the magnitude of academic placement decline in their specific field

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your primary career goal — academic faculty position, industry role, or are you genuinely uncertain?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student's field and program selection is calibrated to a realistic outcome or to a minority outcome that requires explicit above-average program performance to achieve
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If academic: ask which field, then cross-reference that field's current academic placement rate and 20-year trend from NSF SED data
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If industry or uncertain: assess whether the chosen field has low-friction industry transition (CS/Engineering) or high-friction transition (biology, humanities) and whether the student has modeled that cost

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you know what percentage of graduates from your target program obtained tenure-track faculty positions in the last 5 years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has done program-level due diligence versus relying on reputation, rankings, or advisor anecdote — and whether the program is above or below the 30% national benchmark threshold
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they know: verify whether the number is above 30% (above-average) and whether it is tenure-track specifically or includes all academic positions including postdocs and adjunct roles
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they don't know: this is a critical data gap; they are making a major life decision without the most directly relevant outcome metric for their stated goal

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you accounted for postdoc years in your financial and career timeline planning, and do you know the postdoc rate in your specific field?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student understands that in biology (57.8%), geosciences (64.2%), and physical sciences (46.5%) the postdoc is structurally mandatory, not optional, and adds 3-5 years to time-to-career
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: ask whether their financial planning, visa situation, and personal timeline can sustain 10-12 years from bachelor's to independent career at postdoc-level salary
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: this is a fundamental planning error; recalculate time-to-career and financial requirements before committing to the program

diagnostic_questions.question: When did your primary advisor or role model enter academia, and have you cross-referenced their career advice against current NSF or equivalent placement data?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student is relying on potentially outdated guidance from an advisor whose academic hiring experience predates the major structural shift in the market (pre-2010 especially)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they have cross-referenced: assess whether they understand the 20-year trend and have adjusted their planning accordingly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they haven't: the student may be making decisions based on a mental model that is 15-20 years out of date, when academic placements were 20 percentage points higher than today

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your contingency plan if you do not obtain an academic position, and has your target program structured support for non-academic career paths?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has a realistic fallback that accounts for field-specific transition friction, or whether the contingency is vague and unmodeled — and whether the program actively supports or culturally discourages non-academic paths
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they have a specific plan: evaluate whether it accounts for retraining costs in biology, identity/cultural shift in humanities, or whether it is seamless as in CS/Engineering
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no plan: in fields where academic placement is now below 30-34%, the contingency is not a backup scenario but a near-majority outcome that requires as much planning as the primary path

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the definite commitment rate for graduates in your target field at graduation — not eventual employment, but committed plans on the day of degree conferral?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The actual baseline probability of having a clear next step at graduation, which is the most honest signal of career risk in the field
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they know: check whether they understand that humanities (65.8%) and biomedical (68.2%) mean more than 1 in 3 graduates face genuine uncertainty at graduation, and have planned for that scenario
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they don't know: introduce this as the most direct available metric of graduation-day career risk, more honest than vague 'employment rate' figures that programs typically advertise

industry_realities.common_belief: Most PhD graduates go into academic careers — that's the primary outcome the PhD prepares you for
industry_realities.actual_reality: In 2023, industry/business (47%) surpassed academia (34%) as the primary destination for new S&E PhD graduates; this is now the structural norm, not an exception or a fallback
industry_realities.implication: Students and programs that frame industry as the backup path are operating in an inverted reality; the majority outcome is now industry, and academic placement is the minority, above-average outcome

industry_realities.common_belief: The academic job market is tough but PhD graduates who work hard enough will find faculty positions eventually
industry_realities.actual_reality: Academic placements have declined 20 percentage points across all S&E fields over 20 years (54% in 2003 to 34% in 2023), with some fields like math/statistics dropping 43 percentage points; this is a structural, multi-decade contraction, not a temporary cycle
industry_realities.implication: The academic job market is not going to recover to historical norms; students must plan for a structurally smaller academic job market, not treat current conditions as a temporary trough

industry_realities.common_belief: A postdoc in biology is an optional step you take if you want to do more research before industry
industry_realities.actual_reality: 57.8% of biology/biomedical PhDs go directly to postdocs — it is a mandatory structural step before competitive candidacy for permanent faculty positions, not an optional research extension
industry_realities.implication: Biology PhD career timelines must include 3-5 mandatory postdoc years; the real time-to-independent-career is 10-12 years from bachelor's, not the 5-6 years implied by PhD completion alone

industry_realities.common_belief: Program prestige and advisor reputation are the best proxies for your career outcomes as a PhD graduate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Field-level structural forces — postdoc mandates, academic placement rates, definite commitment rates at graduation — create baseline outcome probabilities that prestige modifies but does not override; most biology labs produce 10+ PhDs per tenure-track slot regardless of advisor fame
industry_realities.implication: Students must evaluate field-level career structure and program-specific placement rates, not just prestige rankings; a prestigious program in a field with 27% academic placement (math/stats 2023) still produces mostly non-academic graduates

industry_realities.common_belief: If my target program says their graduates are all employed, the career outcomes are strong
industry_realities.actual_reality: 'Eventually employed' and 'had definite plans at graduation' are dramatically different metrics; humanities (65.8%) and biomedical (68.2%) definite commitment rates mean more than 1 in 3 graduates have no committed plans on graduation day, even if most eventually find something
industry_realities.implication: Request definite commitment rates at graduation — not eventual employment statistics — when evaluating program outcomes; the gap between the two metrics reveals the real level of uncertainty graduates face at the moment it matters most

industry_realities.common_belief: If academia doesn't work out, a PhD in any field can transition to industry without significant friction
industry_realities.actual_reality: CS/Engineering PhD to industry is near-seamless; biology PhD to industry often requires retraining or skills reframing; humanities PhD to non-academic careers involves a cultural and identity shift that programs actively discourage rather than support
industry_realities.implication: Field selection is a decision about career optionality, not just intellectual interest; the friction cost of non-academic transition must be modeled as part of the PhD decision, not assumed away

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they assess academic career viability
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes academic career is the default expected outcome of a PhD, treats industry as the fallback, and relies on advisor anecdote or program reputation as evidence of career viability
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Looks up field-specific NSF SED academic placement rates and 20-year trends; notes that academia is now the minority outcome (34%) and that the trend has been consistently downward for two decades; treats academic placement as an above-average outcome to be planned and earned, not assumed
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who assume academic careers are the default will be blindsided by a market where 66% of S&E PhDs go elsewhere; senior thinkers plan for the structural majority outcome while explicitly strategizing for the minority academic outcome

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they account for postdoc years in career planning
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats PhD completion as the career start date; financial and timeline planning ends at degree conferral; postdoc is seen as a choice or bonus research period
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Builds total time-to-independent-career into planning from day one; for biology, models 10-12 years from bachelor's including 3-5 mandatory postdoc years at $52,000-$65,000/year; treats the postdoc as a structural cost, not a choice
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who don't model postdoc years will face compounding financial and personal disruption that was entirely predictable from public data; the cost is avoidable with accurate upfront planning

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Which career outcome metric they use to evaluate programs
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Accepts 'our graduates all get jobs' or general employment rates as evidence of strong outcomes; does not distinguish between eventual employment, employment at graduation, tenure-track versus adjunct, or postdoc versus permanent position
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Demands definite commitment rates at graduation by field and program; distinguishes tenure-track from all academic positions; asks for 5-year placement data specific to tenure-track roles; recognizes that 65-68% definite commitment rates signal genuine graduation-day uncertainty
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The difference between 'eventually employed' and 'had committed plans at graduation' can represent years of uncertainty and financial instability; using the right metric changes program selection decisions materially

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they use advisor guidance on the academic job market
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats advisor career experience as the primary or most reliable source of job market information; does not cross-reference with external data or consider when the advisor entered academia
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Notes when advisor entered academia; if pre-2010, applies a strong discount to their job market descriptions; cross-references all advisor guidance against current NSF SED data; understands that a 2005 academic hire experienced a market where 54% of S&E PhDs went to academia versus 34% today
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: An advisor's job market experience from 2005 is structurally inapplicable to 2025 planning; students who don't make this correction will build plans on a 20-percentage-point overestimate of academic placement probability

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they think about field selection relative to career optionality
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Selects field based primarily on intellectual interest and assumes career pivots between field and industry are straightforward if needed; does not model transition friction
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Explicitly models the friction cost of non-academic transition by field before committing; weights CS/Engineering's near-zero friction versus biology's retraining requirement versus humanities' cultural identity shift; treats career optionality as a first-order decision variable alongside intellectual interest
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who discover post-PhD that their field has high non-academic transition friction face years of additional retraining or identity negotiation that was entirely predictable at the selection stage
